lessons.title: Components of a Drip Irrigation System
lessons.body: A drip irrigation system delivers water directly to plant roots through a network of tubes and emitters. The main components are: water source (well, tank, or tap), pump (if needed), filter, mainline, sub-mainline, drip lines (laterals), emitters, and fittings (connectors, valves, end caps). For a smallholder in Africa, a typical system might use a 200-litre drum elevated 1 metre to provide gravity pressure. You'll need a filter to prevent cloggingâa 120-mesh screen filter is common. The mainline is usually 32mm or 25mm PVC or PE pipe, while drip lines are 16mm. Emitters can be built into the drip line (inline) or inserted separately (online). Valves control water flow to different sections. End caps close the drip lines. A simple system for a 10m x 10m vegetable plot might cost $50-$100. Start with a kit that includes all parts. Remember: without a filter, emitters clog quickly, especially with dirty water. Also, a pressure regulator (1-2 bar) protects the system. In Africa, many farmers use gravity-fed systems from tanks to save on pumps. You can also use a bucket kit for very small plots. The key is to match components to your water source and field size. Always use black polyethylene tubing to prevent algae growth. Keep spare parts like extra emitters and connectors. This system saves water and labour compared to watering cans.

lessons.title: Choosing Drip Emitters and Tubing
lessons.body: Choosing the right emitters and tubing is crucial for efficient drip irrigation. Emitters come in different flow rates: 1, 2, 4, or 8 litres per hour (L/h). For vegetables like tomatoes, peppers, and onions, 2 L/h emitters spaced 30-40 cm apart are ideal. For sandy soil, use higher flow (4 L/h) because water spreads less. For clay soil, lower flow (1-2 L/h) prevents runoff. Tubing: drip lines are typically 16mm diameter. You can buy inline drip tape (thin wall, cheap, lasts 1-2 seasons) or thick-walled drip line (lasts 5-10 years). In Africa, UV-resistant drip tape is important because sunlight degrades cheap tape quickly. Space emitters according to crop spacing: for maize, 30 cm; for leafy greens, 20 cm. You can also use adjustable online emitters if you want to change flow. But they are more expensive and prone to clogging. For a smallholder, start with a 16mm inline drip line with 2 L/h emitters at 30 cm spacing. That gives about 6.6 emitters per metre. For a 10m row, that's 66 emitters, delivering 132 L/h. If you have 10 rows, you need 1320 L/h. Check your water source can supply that. Tubing connectors: use barbed fittings for 16mm. Always use a punch tool to make holes for online emittersânever a nail. Also, consider pressure-compensating (PC) emitters if your field slopes or laterals are long. They cost more but ensure even watering. For most smallholders, non-PC is fine if laterals are under 30m. Buy from reputable dealers to avoid clogging from poor quality.

lessons.title: Designing a Simple Drip Layout for Vegetables
lessons.body: Designing a drip layout starts with a sketch of your plot. Measure length and width. For vegetables, rows are typically 30-50 cm apart. Let's design for a 10m x 10m plot with tomatoes. Rows: 10m long, spaced 50 cm apart, so 20 rows. Each row gets one drip line. Total drip line length = 20 x 10m = 200m. Use 16mm drip line with 2 L/h emitters at 30 cm spacing. Each row has 33 emitters (10m / 0.3m â 33). Total emitters = 20 x 33 = 660. Water demand: 660 x 2 L/h = 1320 L/h. If you run the system for 1 hour, you apply 1320 litres. That's about 13.2 mm of water over 100 mÂ² (since 1 mm = 1 L/mÂ², and 100 mÂ² = 100 L per mm). Tomatoes need about 5-7 mm per day. So you might run for 30-40 minutes daily. Now, mainline: from water source to the field. Use 32mm PVC or PE. Sub-mainline runs along the top of rows. Connect drip lines to sub-mainline with barbed connectors and a small valve for each row (optional). Or use a manifold. For gravity systems, elevate tank 1-2m. For 1320 L/h, you need a tank outlet of at least 25mm. If using a pump, choose one that delivers 1500 L/h at 1 bar. Always include a filter after the pump or tank. Also, install a pressure regulator if pressure exceeds 2 bar. End each drip line with a flush valve for cleaning. This layout is simple and scalable. For a 20m x 20m plot, double everything. Keep laterals under 30m to avoid pressure loss. If slope is steep, use pressure-compensating emitters or run laterals along contours.

lessons.title: Installing a Drip System: Step-by-Step
lessons.body: Installing a drip system is straightforward if you follow these steps. Step 1: Gather toolsâpipe cutter, punch tool, barbed connectors, filter, valves, end caps, and Teflon tape. Step 2: Position your water source. If using a tank, place it on a stand at least 1m high. Step 3: Install the filter and mainline. Connect filter to tank outlet. Use 32mm PVC pipe for mainline. Run it to the field. Step 4: Lay out sub-mainline. This is a 16mm or 25mm pipe that runs along the top of your rows. Connect it to mainline with a reducer and valve. Step 5: Install drip lines. Unroll drip line along each row. Cut to length, leaving 30cm extra. Connect one end to sub-mainline using a barbed connector. Fold the other end and secure with an end cap or figure-8 clamp. Step 6: Punch holes for online emitters only if using blank tubing. For inline drip line, skip this. Step 7: Flush the system before installing emitters. Remove end caps and run water for 2 minutes to clear debris. Step 8: Install end caps. Step 9: Test the system. Turn on water and check for leaks and even flow. Adjust pressure regulator if needed. Step 10: Bury or secure drip lines lightly with soil or pegs to prevent movement. For a 10m x 10m plot, this takes 2-3 hours. Always use a punch tool for holesânever a nail. Use Teflon tape on threaded connections. In Africa, protect drip lines from animals by fencing or raising them slightly. After installation, run the system daily and check for clogged emitters. Keep a repair kit with extra connectors and emitters. If you have a pump, install a pressure gauge to monitor. Remember: a well-installed system saves water and increases yields.

lessons.title: Filtering and Maintaining Drip Systems
lessons.body: Filters are the most important part of a drip system because emitters clog easily. Use a 120-mesh screen filter for clean water, or a 200-mesh for very clean water. If your water source is a river or dam, use a sand filter first, then a screen filter. Clean the screen filter weekly: remove the screen, rinse with clean water, and replace. If you see a pressure drop, clean it immediately. For sand filters, backwash every 2-4 weeks. Maintenance also includes flushing drip lines. Once a month, remove end caps and run water for 5 minutes to flush out sediment. If emitters clog, remove them and soak in a 1% chlorine solution (household bleach) for 30 minutes, then rinse. For inline drip tape, you can inject chlorine at 1-2 ppm continuously for 30 minutes to clear organic matter. But be careful: too much chlorine damages crops. Use a fertilizer injector or a simple bucket with a valve. Also, check for leaks: walk the system weekly and fix with repair couplings. In Africa, rodents and insects can chew drip lines. Use traps or raise lines on stakes. After harvest, drain and store drip lines in a cool, dark place. If you use drip tape, it may last only one season; thick-walled drip line lasts 5-10 years. Keep a log of maintenance activities. A well-maintained system can last a decade. Remember: clean water in, clean water out. Never use dirty water without filtration. If you have algae, use a 0.5% copper sulfate solution, but only for non-crop periods. Always follow safety guidelines when handling chemicals.

lessons.title: Fertigation: Injecting Nutrients through Drip
lessons.body: Fertigation is the practice of injecting soluble fertilizers into your drip system. It saves labour and delivers nutrients directly to roots. Common fertilizers: urea, potassium nitrate, calcium nitrate, and NPK blends. Use only fully soluble fertilizersânever use granular or organic fertilizers that can clog emitters. A simple venturi injector costs $20-$50 and works with a pump or gravity system. For gravity, use a bucket with a valve and a small pump, or a bypass tank. Mix fertilizer at recommended rates: for tomatoes, apply 5-10 g of NPK (20-20-20) per plant per week during fruiting. Dissolve in a bucket of water, then inject over 30 minutes. Always inject after a plain water flush to avoid burning roots. Then flush again with clean water for 10 minutes. Never mix calcium with phosphate or sulfate fertilizersâthey precipitate and clog. Use a separate injection for each. In Africa, many farmers use urea (46-0-0) for leafy greens: 3-5 g per plant per week. For fertigation, you need a filter after the injector to catch any undissolved particles. Also, use a backflow preventer to protect your water source. Fertigation schedule: apply nutrients 2-3 times per week during peak growth. Monitor plant leaves for deficiency symptoms. If you see yellowing, adjust. Keep a log of fertilizer types and amounts. Over-fertilization can burn plants and pollute groundwater. Start with half the recommended rate and increase. Always wear gloves and goggles when handling fertilizers. After fertigation, flush the system thoroughly. This method can increase yields by 20-30% compared to broadcasting. It's ideal for smallholders because it saves fertilizer and water.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a filter in a drip irrigation system?
options: B) To prevent emitters from clogging
quiz.explanation: Filters remove debris and particles that can block emitters.

quiz.q: Which component provides pressure in a gravity-fed drip system?
quiz.explanation: An elevated tank uses gravity to create water pressure.

quiz.q: What is the typical diameter of drip line tubing for smallholder systems?
quiz.explanation: 16mm is the standard diameter for drip lines in smallholder systems.

quiz.q: Which emitter flow rate is best for sandy soil?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soil has low water holding capacity, so higher flow rates like 4 L/h are better.

quiz.q: What spacing of emitters is recommended for tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes typically require 30-40 cm emitter spacing for adequate water coverage.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of pressure-compensating (PC) emitters?
options: B) They provide even watering on slopes
quiz.explanation: PC emitters maintain consistent flow regardless of pressure variations, ensuring even watering.

quiz.q: How many emitters are needed for a 10m row with 30 cm spacing?
quiz.explanation: 10m divided by 0.3m per emitter gives approximately 33 emitters.

quiz.q: What is the total water demand for 660 emitters at 2 L/h?
quiz.explanation: 660 emitters Ã 2 L/h = 1320 L/h.

quiz.q: How long should you run a drip system to apply 5 mm of water to a 100 mÂ² plot?
quiz.explanation: 5 mm over 100 mÂ² requires 500 L. At 1320 L/h, it takes about 23 minutes, closest to 30 minutes.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mainline diameter for a small drip system?
quiz.explanation: 32mm mainline is common for smallholder systems to reduce pressure loss.

quiz.q: What tool should be used to punch holes for online emitters?
quiz.explanation: A punch tool makes clean holes without damaging the tubing.

quiz.q: What should you do before installing end caps on drip lines?
quiz.explanation: Flushing removes debris that could clog emitters.

quiz.q: How often should you clean a screen filter?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning prevents clogging and maintains flow.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mesh size for a screen filter with clean water?
quiz.explanation: 120-mesh is standard for clean water sources.

quiz.q: What should you do if emitters clog with organic matter?
options: D) Use a nail to clear
quiz.explanation: Soaking in 1% chlorine solution clears organic clogs.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of drip line damage in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Rodents and insects often chew drip lines, causing leaks.

quiz.q: How long can thick-walled drip line last with proper maintenance?
quiz.explanation: Thick-walled drip line is durable and can last 5-10 years.

quiz.q: What is fertigation?
options: A) Applying fertilizer with irrigation water
quiz.explanation: Fertigation is the injection of soluble fertilizers into irrigation water.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is suitable for fertigation?
quiz.explanation: Potassium nitrate is fully soluble and safe for drip systems.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of NPK (20-20-20) per tomato plant per week during fruiting?
quiz.explanation: 5-10 g per plant per week is a common recommendation for tomatoes.

quiz.q: Why should you not mix calcium with phosphate fertilizers?
quiz.explanation: Calcium and phosphate react to form precipitates that clog emitters.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a backflow preventer in fertigation?
options: B) To protect water source from contamination
quiz.explanation: A backflow preventer stops fertilizer from contaminating the water source.

quiz.q: How often should you fertigate during peak growth?
quiz.explanation: 2-3 times per week is typical for peak nutrient demand.

quiz.q: What should you do after fertigation?
options: A) Flush the system with clean water
quiz.explanation: Flushing prevents fertilizer residue from clogging emitters.

quiz.q: What is a venturi injector used for?
quiz.explanation: A venturi injector draws fertilizer solution into the irrigation water.

quiz.q: What is the first step in installing a drip system?
quiz.explanation: Installing the filter and mainline is the first step after positioning the water source.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a pressure regulator?
quiz.explanation: A pressure regulator keeps pressure within the optimal range for emitters.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for drip lines in a vegetable plot?
quiz.explanation: 30-50 cm spacing matches typical vegetable row spacing.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using inline drip tape?
options: A) It is cheap and easy to install
quiz.explanation: Inline drip tape is inexpensive and simple to use, though it may last only one season.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see a pressure drop in your drip system?
quiz.explanation: A pressure drop often indicates a clogged filter, which should be cleaned.
